country.comment: The study focuses on rural water supply systems and sanitation policy in Brazil, drawing particularly on institutional experiences with the Integrated Rural Sanitation System (SISAR) in the state of Ceará and interviews held in Fortaleza, Ceará.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF pp. 2-3, Section 1; PDF p. 4, Section 2.2

effect_estimate.comment: No primary quantitative causal or associative effect estimate on household or community water access outcomes is estimated (background text cites secondary data showing SISAR covers 1,419 communities and 611,252 rural inhabitants, or 32% of Ceará's rural population). Primary empirical results consist of binary expert-panel agreement counts across 14 proposed governance strategies.
effect_estimate.value: Expert-panel validation (no numeric effect estimate on water access outcomes reported): Among 11 rural water and sanitation specialists evaluating 14 proposed multiscale strategies (using an >80% agreement threshold), 13 strategies were endorsed — 4 of 5 at the national level (11/11 for a national universal water/investment plan, 11/11 for strengthening local institutions, 10/11 for recognizing community organizations, 10/11 for national institutional articulation; 5/11 in favor vs. 6/11 against creating a national rural water council), all 7 at the local/regional level (9/11 to 11/11 in favor, including 11/11 for municipal plans covering rural communities, 10/11 for planning/contracting/regulatory/support instruments, 10/11 for forming associations and local water regulations, and 9/11 for municipality-community association legal instruments), and both 2 at the community level (10/11 for legislative water quality surveillance and 10/11 for tariff setting aligned with socioeconomic and hydrological conditions).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 5, Section 2.3; PDF pp. 6-9, Sections 3.1-3.3, Tables 2-5

mechanism_certainty.comment: Ceiling is at most 2 for non-experimental/non-quasi-experimental designs. Coded 0 because the study does not empirically measure or observe a legal/administrative mechanism operating on primary water access outcomes ( nor test a statistical association with outcomes); instead, it synthesizes secondary literature/SISAR reports and elicits normative expert agreement (N=11) on proposed multiscale strategies posited to improve sustainability and universal rural water access.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines urban-rural policy dichotomy and inclusion of rural areas in national/state/municipal sanitation plans (ELIGIBILITY: planning, service_area); user tariff setting according to ability to pay and lifecycle cost-recovery subsidies (BURDEN: fees); community-managed water supply associations, formalization/legal instruments, multi-tier coordination, and post-construction technical/administrative support such as SISAR (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination, bureaucratic_assistance); and service cuts for non-payment/compliance with local regulations (ENFORCEMENT: disconnection).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, planning, service_area, fees, disconnection, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination, bureaucratic_assistance
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 2-4, Section 1 & Table 1; PDF pp. 6-9, Sections 3.1-3.3 & Tables 2-5

outcome_flags.comment: Focuses on universal rural drinking water access and coverage deficits, compliance with legislative drinking water quality standards, tariff/subsidy affordability relative to ability to pay, and long-term operational functionality/continuity (including cuts for default).
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 1-4, Abstract, Section 1 & Table 1; PDF pp. 6-9, Sections 3.1-3.3 & Tables 2-5

publication_year.comment: Published 14 June 2023 in MDPI Water (Volume 15, Article 2232).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary empirical data collection consists of face-to-face interviews with 11 rural water and sanitation specialists evaluating proposed institutional strategies (combined with literature review and institutional case synthesis of SISAR in Ceará). Although expert responses were tallied as binary yes/no agreement counts (>80% cutoff), there is no analytical cross-sectional exposure-outcome testing and only one primary component, making CASP Qualitative Checklist the closest design-matched tool.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 2, Section 1; PDF pp. 3-5, Sections 2.1-2.3

sample_size.comment: Section 2.1 also notes a prior study involving 88 specialists ([17]/[24]) from which Table 1's critical factors were drawn, whereas 11 specialists with >=10 years of experience (3 federal, 7 state, 1 municipal) were interviewed as the primary sample for this study.
sample_size.value: 11 specialists (experts in rural water and sanitation interviewed face-to-face)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 3, Section 2.1; PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 2.2-2.3

study_design.comment: Combines non-systematic literature review and secondary institutional lessons from Ceará's SISAR model (and prior critical-factor rankings) with primary face-to-face structured expert interviews (11 specialists voting yes/no on 14 proposed national, local, and community strategies, retaining items with >80% agreement).
study_design.value: Literature and institutional case synthesis (SISAR in Ceará) combined with a structured expert-panel evaluation via face-to-face interviews (yes/no agreement survey)
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 2, Section 1; PDF pp. 3-5, Sections 2.1-2.3 & Figure 1
